Meeting header
Date: 2026-11-01 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Miguel Ortega (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Redwood SE), Elena Martinez (Sierra Head of ML), Victor Huang (Platform), Priya Raman (SRE), Markus Lee (Data Eng)

Auto-summary (auto gen, may be rough):
We dug into approaches for sustaining 128k+ prompts with acceptable p95 latency for interactive features. Covered chunking strategies (append vs windowed), attention fallthrough, KV cache tiering and eviction, batching configurations to keep GPU utilization high without blowing latency SLOs, and quantization options that reduce memory but affect perf. Discussed on-prem / VPC constraints (peering, HSM/KMS, data egress) and a path for a scoped pilot + benchmark.

Topics: chunking strategies; KV tiering & eviction; attention sharding; batching SLOs; quantization tradeoffs; private deployment networking and KMS/HSM; next-step benchmarks

Action items (captured above)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samira: okay thanks everyone for joining, we'll kick off — I'm Samira from Redwood, I'll run the agenda. Miguel's going to deep dive into the runtime ops and then we can jump to the network/on-prem pieces.
[00:18] Elena: yep thanks, our goal today is to understand how we can support documents that exceed 100k tokens so we can power longform analytics. Key constraints: 95th percentile latency under 2.5s for interactive reads, and persistent KV so that we don't reingest.
[00:35] Miguel: got it, and hi everyone. Quick note: our terminology, when I say "KV cache" I sometimes say "kayvee" — transcript may show different. We'll talk about multi-tier KV, eviction policies and lazy loading.
[00:52] Victor: timeline is tight, we have compliance review mid-November and a pilot by end of month would be ideal.
[01:05] Aisha: quick plug — we already prepared a sample 128k trace from your anonymized corpus, Markus provided that, Miguel ran it locally. We'll share the run.
[01:20] Markus: yeah sent via dropbox earlier, sorry if the path's messy.
[01:28] Miguel: cool, so the big levers for 128k are: chunking (how you append vs window), attention strategy (global vs local vs sparse windows), KV caching and tiering, and runtime batching. If you pick the wrong mix you either blow memory or you blow P95.
[01:50] Elena: can you give a concrete pipeline example?
[01:55] Miguel: sure. Example A: append-based stream — you keep appending chunks to history and maintain a persistent KV for prefix tokens. For 128k you want to avoid repeatedly recomputing early layers; so we use prefix caching and a read-through eviction policy. Example B: sliding-window + summary — you keep a short soft window for attention and summarize older context to compact embedding. Each has different latency/cost shapes.
[02:28] Victor: what about attention fallthrough? we've seen spikes when the model crosses certain sequence breaks.
[02:36] Miguel: yep that's the fallthrough — when the attention computation can't fit optimized kernels and falls back to a slower path. We see it around model-token boundaries usually when sequence length crosses GPU-friendly tiling. On our runtime we try to tile and shard attention to avoid that.
[02:58] Samira: Miguel, can you sketch the eviction tiers you recommended?
[03:03] Miguel: sure. Tier 0: in-GPU KV hotset (recently used and needed for low-latency). Tier 1: host DRAM for warm entries (fast CPU-GPU transfers with pinned memory). Tier 2: remote Redis-like store or SSD-backed tier for cold KV. Eviction policy: LRU-ish but weighted by recency and predicted future access using simple heuristics from our workload profiler. We also support pinned keys for customer-specified anchors.
[03:36] Elena: pinned keys is critical — we have sections that must always be present. How durable is the host DRAM tier on restart?
[03:44] Miguel: host DRAM is ephemeral per node; we rely on a write-through to Tier 2 for durability. On restart, the runtime can stream back hot keys from Tier 2 or pre-warm using a precomputed snapshot. That's why we recommend snapshotting after large uploads or indexing operations.
[04:06] Priya: any security concerns for Tier 2 if it's remote? we have strict encryption and KMS rules.
[04:12] Aisha: we can integrate customer KMS/HSM for encryption-at-rest and in-transit; the Private deployment option supports customer-managed keys and HSM attestation. For hosted we have our KMS but can get SOC2 reports and attestations.
[04:30] Elena: we'll need the SOC2 artifact and an HSM integration note — please include that in the follow-up.
[04:36] Samira: noted.
[04:40] [05:00] Miguel: moving on to batching — continuous batching helps throughput but it adds queuing latency. For interactive SLOs you tune the batch timeout and max batch size; also do dynamic batching that adapts based on request CDF. For long tokens, we do per-chunk batching: new requests with short appended chunks can ride on partially-filled batches.
[05:22] Victor: are there heuristics you recommend? like max-batch 16 for p95 under 3s?
[05:27] Miguel: it's workload-dependent. For your trace we saw good results with batch sizes 8-12 and dynamic timeout 12-18ms; bigger batches improved throughput but increased tail. We'll include the exact csv with p50/p95/tokens-per-second.
[05:42] Elena: quantization: can we use 4-bit across model and keep perf? we're trying to reduce memory footprint to fit more KV on device.
[05:51] Miguel: short version: we support Q4 variants but 4-bit introduces some kernel path differences — some attention kernels run slower in 4-bit because of additional packing/unpacking. We recommend mixed strategy: int8/Q4 for MLP layers and keep attention in higher precision if you're latency-sensitive. For extremely memory constrained we can go full Q4 but you'll see slight quality and latency tradeoffs.
[06:20] Samira: we also provide per-workload quantization recommendations — Miguel will send a matrix: model layer vs quant mode vs kernel performance.
[06:28] Markus: any chance of doing QAT (quant-aware tuning) on our side?
[06:32] Miguel: QAT helps but it's a longer path. We can do post-training quant and provide guidance. QAT works best if you can invest a few days of fine-tuning on representative prompts.
[06:44] [07:00] Victor: about on-prem: we need to understand network egress and peering. If we run Redwood Private control plane in our VPC, what's the data flow?
[07:12] Aisha: in the Private model we run a customer-controlled control plane that manages runtime in their VPC; model shards live in your subnet and the control plane orchestrates. For hosted fallback you can restrict egress via firewall rules. We support VPC peering and direct connect options. Also, no data leaves your VPC unless configured for telemetry.
[07:34] Elena: and KMS? we need to use our HSM for key wraps.
[07:39] Aisha: yes supported via customer-provided KMS; we support AWS CloudHSM and common HSM vendors via KMIP. We'll send the integration doc.
[07:49] [08:00] Miguel: an important runtime note: for very long context we use incremental KV application — only apply transformer layers to newly-attended tokens and reuse cached hidden states for earlier tokens. That reduces compute significantly, but it requires careful cache invalidation when you run rollouts or update model weights.
[08:22] Markus: how do you handle model rollouts? if we bump model version, does the cache get invalidated?
[08:27] Miguel: by default yes. We support versioned KV namespaces and can do a gradual migration: keep old namespace for warm sessions, spawn new namespace for incoming sessions and background-migrate hot keys. That avoids a cold-slam.
[08:45] Elena: curious about attention sharding — does Redwood split attention across GPUs for a single request?
[08:50] Miguel: yes we support sharding. Two approaches: layer-shard (each GPU holds different layers) and head-shard (split attention heads across devices). For long context we often use block-sharding where sequences are chunked and attention computed with overlap windows to approximate global attention. There's also an offload path where KV stays on CPU and we stream windows to GPU.
[09:16] Priya: overlap windows — that sounds like you can get eventual consistency problems with boundary tokens?
[09:22] Miguel: you need overlap equal to attention radius to avoid blind spots. We also use cross-block smoothing to reduce artifacts. It's not perfect but empirically works well and trades off compute for memory.
[09:36] [10:00] Elena: any oddball perf cliffs we should be aware of?
[10:04] Miguel: yes: kernel fallthrough (mentioned earlier), fragmentation from many small KV entries, and network spikes during pre-warm which can cause transient latency bursts. Also attention cache growth can lead to OOM if chunking isn't tuned. We put alarms on cache pressure and provide automatic rollback to a safe config.
[10:26] Victor: curious about autoscaling — if we autoscale the GPU pool during load, do clients experience re-routing latency?
[10:32] Miguel: short answer: small blips. We drain connections gracefully and route to warmed nodes when possible. For heavy stateful sessions we recommend reserved capacity (Dedicated) to avoid re-sharding costs during piloting.
[10:50] Samira: that matches the earlier discussion about Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs. Dedicated gives you pinned GPU and KV locality but increases cost. Hosted is cheaper but you may hit eviction or tiering more often.
[11:06] [11:30] Elena: can you walk through a sample profiling output? what's in your csv?
[11:33] Miguel: sure the csv has columns: timestamp, request_id, sequence_len, chunks_sent, batch_size, kernel_path, gpu_util, p50, p95 latency, kv_hits, kv_misses, bytes_egr. For your sample run we saw >85% kv_hit rate for hot sessions and p95 around 1.9s with tuned batch and tiering.
[11:57] Markus: what does bytes_egr look like for pre-warm?
[12:00] Miguel: pre-warm can burst tens to low hundreds of MB depending on how much KV you hydrate; that's why we recommend staged pre-warm and rate-limit the stream if over a WAN link.
[12:12] Priya: about observability — what traces/tags do you emit for compliance?
[12:17] Aisha: we emit per-request traces, token counts, KV operations, model version, node id; logs can be forwarded to customer S3 or SIEM. We can also suppress pii via a redact pipeline.
[12:31] [13:00] Elena: can you describe a realistic pilot plan steps?
[13:05] Samira: quick plan: 1) exchange topology and sample traces (done) 2) Redwood runs a baseline in our hosted sandbox with your traces (Redwood se) 3) compare metrics and tune batch/quant configs 4) deploy Private trial in your VPC with a small cluster and run on-prem benchmark 5) expand to Dedicated when satisfied. We'll attach timelines.
[13:33] Victor: length of pilot? 2-3 weeks?
[13:36] Samira: typical pilot 2-4 weeks for long-context workloads given tuning iterations.
[13:41] [14:00] Miguel: got a screenshot in the shared doc that shows kernel paths flipping at 64k and 96k — that's the fallthrough I mentioned. I'll highlight that in the benchmark csv.
[14:10] Elena: any quick mitigations to avoid the 96k cliff?
[14:13] Miguel: yes: enforce chunk size that keeps per-kernel tiling aligned, or force an attention-sparse variant for the expensive layers. Also you can enable a hybrid attention that uses local + summary tokens for global positions.
[14:34] Priya: can we set hard upper limits on tokens per request? we might want to reject or queue huge ones.
[14:39] Aisha: yes policy engine supports per-tenant limits and graceful rejection messages and fallback endpoints.
[14:50] [15:00] Markus: how about cost modeling? if we go Dedicated with 4xA100 equiv, what's per 1M tokens cost roughly?
[15:10] Samira: we gave a rough estimate in the deck but Miguel will produce a more precise cost model: cost = infra + model flops + storage + ops. For long context a big portion is memory and I/O. We'll send a cost sheet.
[15:25] Victor: do you support spot or preemptible?
[15:28] Miguel: for Dedicated we don't recommend spot for hot sessions. You can use spot for batch jobs or background indexing.
[15:35] [16:00] Elena: security review pointer again — we need SOC2, encryption at rest/in transit, RBAC and audit logs.
[16:08] Samira: we'll attach the SOC2 report and outline RBAC/SSO flows; Redwood supports SAML/Okta, role-based policies, and audit log shipping.
[16:20] [16:30] Miguel: a couple of gotchas we flagged in the run: your trace had many small near-duplicate contexts which caused fragmentation — we recommend a min-compaction pass during ingest to combine near-duplicates into a single key to reduce KV index blowup.
[16:48] Elena: that makes sense, Markus can run that on the ingestion pipeline.
[16:52] Markus: yes we'll try dedup first.
[16:56] [17:00] Priya: do you have tooling for simulated load from our VPC? we want to emulate WAN latency and peering.
[17:06] Aisha: yes we have a network harness that can be run in your VPC or from our sandbox — it simulates latency, packet loss and warmed pre-warm streams. We'll coordinate to run it during the pilot.
[17:20] Miguel: also note we can provide a lightweight on-prem runtime container for benchmarking that has same runtime kernels but no control plane. It's handy for deterministic latency runs.
[17:34] [18:00] Elena: if we want to keep attention in higher precision and quantize MLPs, what's your expected memory savings?
[18:08] Miguel: ballpark: going from fp16 to q4 on MLP might save ~30-40% memory depending on layer sizes; the attention layers dominate for very long context so savings are limited if attention remains fp16. We'll provide a per-layer table.
[18:30] Victor: and that ties back to how much KV we can keep on-GPU.
[18:33] Miguel: exactly.
[18:36] [19:00] Samira: okay wrapping towards next steps — we'll prepare: benchmark csv, quant recommendation matrix, integration doc for KMS/HSM, and sample pre-warm plan. Sierra will provide a topology diagram and confirm pilot dates.
[19:18] Elena: I'll coordinate internally and get back with a proposed pilot window.
[19:24] Samira: great. Any final quick q's?
[19:28] Priya: one last — do you support per-tenant throttles based on token budget?
[19:33] Aisha: yes token budget, per-route quotas, and pre-emptive throttles.
[19:38] Victor: thanks all, this was useful.
[19:40] [20:00] End of recording.

Meeting recap (manual):
- Redwood recommends a hybrid approach: GPU in-memory hotset + host DRAM warm tier + SSD/remote cold tier with write-through snapshots.
- For 128k+ workloads use chunking with overlap windows and prefix KV caching; avoid kernel fallthrough by tuning chunk sizes and enabling attention-sparse layers when needed.
- Mixed quantization recommended: quantize MLPs first, retain higher precision for attention if latency-critical.
- Private deployment supports customer KMS/HSM; pilot plan includes hosted baseline then on-prem VPC trial.
- Next steps and action items listed above.
